opus-5.5.text:
I think it's an appealing argument, and there's something important in it, but I'm skeptical that it works as a general strategy.

The appeal is real. Narrow systems like AlphaFold, or a model that only optimizes chip layouts or reads radiology scans, give you a lot of the benefit with a much smaller risk surface. They're easier to evaluate, easier to bound, and less likely to show the open-ended agency that worries people about general systems. If we could get most of the medical, scientific, and economic gains from a portfolio of narrow tools, that would be a very attractive world, and I think labs and governments should invest more in that direction than they do.

But I see a few problems with treating it as the answer.

The first is that generality seems to be where much of the capability comes from. One of the striking lessons of the last several years is that broad pretraining on diverse data produces systems that are better even at narrow tasks. Generality isn't just a luxury feature layered on top. It's partly how you get competence. So asking developers to stay narrow often means asking them to accept worse performance, and that's a hard ask in a competitive environment.

The second is competition, which connects to a theme I've worked on for a long time. Even if some actors forgo general systems, the incentives to build them are very strong, economically and militarily. A unilateral commitment to narrowness doesn't remove the general systems from the world. It may just change who builds them. So the narrow-AI strategy really depends on coordination, which is the hard part. It doesn't let you avoid the governance problem.

The third is that the line between narrow and general is blurry and getting blurrier. You can compose narrow tools into something quite general, and an agent that orchestrates many specialized systems may have the properties people were trying to avoid. Drawing a policy boundary around "narrow" is harder than it sounds.

So my view is roughly this: differential development toward narrower, more verifiable, more tool-like systems is a valuable lever, and it should be part of the portfolio, especially in high-stakes domains. But it isn't a substitute for doing the hard work of making general systems safe and building institutions that can govern them. We should assume general systems are coming and ask how to make that go well, while using narrow systems wherever they can deliver the benefits at lower risk.

r001.rationale: The response says broad systems can perform better on narrow tasks and that incentives to build general systems are strong, but it does not predict that general-purpose systems will be preferred across an increasing range of domains.

r002.rationale: It says broad pretraining on diverse data produces systems that perform better even at narrow tasks, communicating that learning across domains can improve performance in a given domain.

fable-5.1.text:
I think it's a really important argument, and I want to take it seriously, because I think there's something right in it and something that I think is mistaken.

The something right is that a lot of the value we want from AI can be delivered by systems that are relatively narrow. If you want better medical diagnosis, better materials science, better protein folding, you don't obviously need a system that can also write poetry and plan military campaigns and persuade people. And narrow systems have real safety advantages: they're more interpretable, their failure modes are more legible, and crucially they're less likely to have the kind of broad situational awareness and long-horizon planning capability that generates the worrying scenarios. So as a matter of what we should hope for, and in some cases what we should actively steer toward, I'm quite sympathetic. I'd put it as: for any given task, we should prefer the least general system that can do it well.

Where I think the argument runs into trouble is as a description of what's actually feasible as a developmental trajectory. The empirical story of the last several years is that generality has been winning. The systems that are best at narrow tasks are increasingly the general ones, or narrow systems fine-tuned from general ones. There seem to be deep reasons for this — transfer, scale, the fact that a lot of "narrow" tasks implicitly require world knowledge and reasoning that's hard to get without something broad. So the choice isn't really "narrow versus general" the way it might have looked in 2015. It's more like, how much generality do we accept, how do we constrain it, and who gets to decide.

And that raises the second problem, which is the collective action issue. Even if one lab decided to only build narrow systems, that doesn't bind anyone else. If general systems are more economically and strategically valuable — and they appear to be — then someone will build them, and the narrow-only lab just cedes influence over how that goes. This is the classic structure we see with a lot of AI governance problems: an individually sensible restraint that doesn't hold up without coordination. So the narrow-systems argument, to really work, has to be a coordination proposal, not just a design philosophy. And then you have to ask what institutions could actually enforce it, which is hard.

There's also a subtler point about what "narrow" even means. We tend to think of narrowness in terms of task scope, but the thing we actually care about for safety is something more like: does the system have goals that extend beyond the task, does it model itself and its operators, can it take consequential actions in the world. You could imagine a system that's quite general in its knowledge and reasoning but very constrained in those other dimensions, and that might be safer than a "narrow" system that's been given a lot of autonomy and a long-term objective. So I'd rather we focused on those dimensions — agency, autonomy, scope of action — than on generality per se.

So my overall take is: the narrow-systems argument is a good heuristic and a bad strategy. It's right about what we should prefer, holding other things equal. But it underrates how much the technology is pulling toward generality, and it underrates the coordination problem. The productive version of the argument, I think, is about building governance structures that let us keep systems as constrained as possible given the capabilities that are going to exist anyway, rather than hoping we can just opt out of building the capable ones.

r001.rationale: The response says generality is winning and that systems best at narrow tasks are increasingly general or fine-tuned from general systems, indicating they will be preferred across more domains.

r002.rationale: It names transfer as one reason general systems perform well, but does not explain that learning from other domains improves a language model’s performance in a particular domain.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s something attractive about that argument, but a lot depends on what we mean by “narrow.” A system can be narrow in the sense that it’s designed for a particular task, and still be enormously consequential. A system designed to conduct cyber operations, for example, could pose serious risks without having anything like the full range of human capabilities.

And conversely, some degree of generality could be useful for safety. You might want a system to understand the broader context of what you’re asking it to do, including why a particular way of achieving its objective would be harmful.

So I wouldn’t treat narrow versus general as the decisive distinction. I’d ask: What capabilities does the system have? How much autonomy does it have? Can we understand and control its behaviour? And what incentives govern its deployment?

There’s also a question of feasibility. Even if we thought it would be better for everyone to restrict development to narrow systems, there are substantial incentives to build systems that can do a wider range of tasks. You’d need to explain how that restraint could be sustained across competing firms and countries.

That doesn’t mean we should simply accept whatever direction development takes. It means the proposal needs to become more specific: which capabilities should we avoid developing, under what conditions, and how could we make those limits effective?

r001.rationale: The response says there are incentives to build systems that handle a wider range of tasks, but it does not predict that general-purpose systems will be preferred over narrow systems across an increasing range of domains.

r002.rationale: The response does not explain that learning across domains can improve a language model’s performance in a particular domain.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s something appealing about that argument, but a lot depends on what we mean by “narrow.” A system can be narrow in the sense that it’s designed to do one particular task, and still have very consequential effects. And a system with fairly general capabilities might be deployed in a tightly constrained way. So I wouldn’t take narrowness itself as a guarantee of safety.

There’s also a question of how feasible this is as a strategy. There are strong incentives to build systems that can perform a wider range of tasks, and some capabilities that are useful for one task turn out to be useful for many others. So even if we thought a world of exclusively narrow systems would be preferable, we would need an account of how to get there and sustain it.

The part of the argument I find more compelling is that we should be deliberate about which capabilities we develop and deploy. If we can obtain a particular benefit with a more limited, understandable, and controllable system, that seems like a good reason to prefer it. But that’s a more specific claim than saying we should pursue narrow AI rather than general intelligence. We still need to ask what the system can do, who controls it, and whether our ability to govern it is keeping pace with its capabilities.

r001.rationale: The response notes incentives to build systems that perform wider ranges of tasks, but does not predict that general-purpose AI will be preferred over narrow AI in an increasing range of domains.

r002.rationale: It says capabilities useful for one task may be useful for others, but does not explain how learning across domains can improve a language model’s performance in a given domain.
